newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel removes equipment from Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel removes equipment from Hebron.

text.p: Israel moved military equipment out of Hebron on Thursday and dismantled guard posts ahead of a handover of most of the West Bank town to Palestinian rule.

The commander of Israeli forces in the West Bank said the army was not redeploying its forces from the town yet but was preparing for orders to do so if parliament approved the handover in a vote expected later on Thursday.
"The removal of the equipment does not change any decision," Major-General Gabi Ofir told army radio. "We are remaining in our usual deployment and on the contrary, have even reinforced our presence.
"But at the same time we are removing some of the equipment and if it is indeed decided we should redeploy, we will keep any timetable necessary."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu crushed a fierce right-wing revolt early on Thursday to win cabinet approval for the Hebron withdrawal pact with the Palestinians.
Ministers accepted the agreement to carry out the long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment by a vote of 11-7 after a stormy meeting lasting 12 hours.
Science Minister Binyamin Begin, son of the late prime minister Menachem Begin, resigned, a cabinet official said.
Begin led the onslaught against Netanyahu for sealing the U.S.-brokered Hebron deal with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday. Arafat's cabinet approved the accord in Gaza.
The wrangling inside Netanyahu's cabinet reflected the deep split in the Likud-led coalition over ceding land to Palestinians that many Israelis believe to be theirs by biblical right.
The agreement was expected to win backing in Israel's parliament later on Thursday thanks to support from the Labour opposition which initiated peace moves with the Palestinians.

An opinion poll in Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper said 67 percent of Israelis were pleased with the Hebron deal. In response to another question, 80 percent said they had not visited Hebron in the last five years.
The poll by Dahaf institute included 504 people and was conducted on Wednesday.

Witnesses in Hebron said a crane was removing an army observation tower from a roof at the northern entrance of the town. The army threw up checkpoints at major intersections around Hebron and many soldiers stood guard.

Soldiers were seen evacuating a building the army had used in the town for years - removing barbed wire, metal sentry boxes, military camp beds and even a wash stand. A flag was removed from the sentry box before it was dismantled, but a soldier hung the flag somewhere else.
The town was shrouded in clouds and driving rain, keeping most of the Palestinians indoors while the signs of 30 years of Israeli occupation were being removed.
"We're very happy to see them go," said Hamed Khalil Amr, watching from his butcher shop. "We hope the settlers will do the same thing and leave our town and let us live in peace," Amr said.
Extra soldiers were on the streets to prevent protests by Jewish settlers who have vowed to stay on in the heart of the city of 100,000 Palestinians.
"It's a sad day when a Jewish government takes this very grave decision," settler Moshe Ben-Zimra said.

"Netanyahu will be remembered as the first prime minister who abandoned the legacy of the fathers to outsiders, who abandoned Jewish lives in the Land of Israel," he told Israel Radio. About 400 militant settlers live in the centre of Hebron, site of the biblical patriarchs, who are revered by Jews and Moslems.

Cabinet secretary Danny Naveh said Israel would soon begin to discuss the principles of so-called "final status" talks to seek a permanent solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. He said Israel hoped to conclude this before the second phase of the further withdrawals.
